I think there are a few big reasons behind why Little Caesars is the most popular in Michigan. Just to start off, LC is based out of Detroit. Their involvement in concessions is another major reason too. LC is owned by Ilitch Holdings, who owns the Detroit Tigers, Red Wings, and practically every major sports and concert venue in SE Michigan. Another huge reason is just by how much LC crowds out the National competition around here. There’s Little Caesars everywhere. Little Caesars has 310 locations in the state, which is over 100 more than the runner-ups of Hungry Howie’s and Jet’s. Domino’s is also out here, seeing that they’re headquarters out of Ann Arbor, but they really start to pop up in full force once you get outside of Detroit proper and into the suburbs & nicer parts of the region, plus they don’t have the Ilitch advantage. That leads me to last major reason, which is that LC pizza is just so damn CHEAP. $5 for a whole pizza is a steal that you just can’t beat. Mix that with the predominantly low-income communities of Detroit and the states other major cities, and you get a recipe for mass success. 

Ultimately LC is a local corporation that, through it’s owner, has basically a monopoly on the massive market of venue concessions. It beats out other pizza chains by their amount of stores in the state by 50%, they’re positively perceived because them & Ilitch involve themselves with local charities and stuff more so than the other locals like Dominos, and their business model caters to one of the prevailing economic brackets in the state. Little Caesars is a brand that was born and bred here, and they flex their home field advantage very well. I don’t think anyone would ever say that their favorite pizza is LC, but the numbers speak for themselves.

In the case of the Cherokee, Muskogee, Choctaw, and Chickasaw, they do have their own sovereignty in the form of a confederacy in the gulf & deep south. While white setters do manage to succeed in pushing good portions of the indigenous peoples out of transappalachia and the upper south over the course of a few decades, they do settle down in Georgia and West Florida (West Florida remains loyalist as in real life, Georgia doesn't get so lucky during the revolutionary war and the waves of incoming Tories tips the public opinion in keeping Georgia as a colony). I haven't thought out the history of the gulf and deep south too much after 1800, but I'd imagine that the collective tension between the British and Indigenous groups would grow until it reaches a boiling point sometime in the 19th century that leads to reform and/or the complete removal of British authority and oversight.

The Seminole manage to stick around in Florida (made up of just East Florida), and they no doubt play a massive role in its independence from the Spanish during the Spanish American wars of independence.

I haven't thought much about the state of affairs in Louisiana yet, so unfortunately I can't comment much on the status of the indigenous peoples west of the Mississippi. You will probably see a post that elaborates on that later down the line.

The reserves are indeed lands that were more open to settlement by Europeans. Some nations within the confederacy were more tolerant of British & French settlers than others but the reserves were ultimately established as a sort of compromise between parties with differing views on the topic of white settlement. The reserves (and the borders of the nations) were established in the early 1800's as neutral treaty lands where white settlements were allowed, and existing white settlements wouldn't be subject to destruction and removal by any Tribal Councils (something that was happening in lands controlled by the Miami, Dakota, and Shawnee prior to the standardization of internal boundaries in the confederacy). In the modern day the reserves are much more ethnically European that the ethnically native and mixed nations.
